title: No beginning to find
hook: count your mothers with twigs, your fathers with balls of clay, and the earth runs out first (SN 15.1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: tears and the four oceans, and your line, be gentle with grief. Today the same chapter opens, with grass and clay and a counting game no one can finish.

Send off a sample of your spit, and you can get back a map of where your great-great-grandparents lived. Go back far enough, though, and the branches multiply faster than anyone can count. Two parents, four grandparents, eight, sixteen, and soon the chart is wider than the page. The Buddha starts the chapter on the long round of lives with a family tree too. But instead of paper, he uses all the grass in India, and then the whole earth.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE BY MAIL.` → `TWO, FOUR, EIGHT, SIXTEEN.` → `NOW USE ALL THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: SN 15.1 opens with a sentence the rest of the chapter keeps returning to. This round of wandering, monks, is without a discoverable beginning. No first point can be found where beings, blocked by not knowing and tied by craving, started roaming. Suppose someone cut all the grass, sticks, branches and leaves in India, gathered them in one heap, and cut them into little sticks four fingers long. Then, laying them down one at a time, they counted: this is my mother, this is my mother's mother. The grass and sticks of India would run out before the line of mothers did. SN 15.2 does the same with the earth. Roll it into balls of clay the size of a jujube seed and lay them down: this is my father, this is my father's father. The earth runs out first. Then the conclusion: for so long you have experienced loss and suffering. It's enough to grow weary of all this, and to be free. The images stretch the mind until it gives up looking for the edge. Not a large number; no number at all. A little later in the same chapter, the Buddha draws out one surprising consequence. It is hard, he says, to find a being who has not at some time been your mother, or your father, your brother, sister, son or daughter. Some Buddhist teachers, in Tibet especially, have built a practice of kindness on that line: anyone you meet may once have been family.
screen: `WITHOUT A DISCOVERABLE BEGINNING` · `GRASS AND STICKS: MY MOTHER'S MOTHER` · `BALLS OF CLAY: MY FATHER'S FATHER` · `ANYONE MAY ONCE HAVE BEEN FAMILY` · then, large: `NO BEGINNING TO FIND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today who isn't family, a coworker, a cashier, a neighbor, someone you find difficult, and picture them clearly. Then gently try the old thought: at some time, in some way, this one may have been my mother, my father, my brother or sister; you don't have to believe it as a fact to let it change how they look. Notice any softening, and rest there with the breath.
Anamatagga. Without a discoverable beginning: the round of lives in SN 15, where the grass of India and the clay of the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers. Today's word.
Your line: anyone may have been family. Even the person you find hardest. Six hundred fifty days now.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism especially, students practice recognizing all beings as having once been their mothers, as a basis for compassion; teachers in other traditions draw on the same chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya.

fork.setup: you're cutting all the grass of India into little sticks, one for each mother back through your line. what happens?
options: the line of mothers and the grass end together.
fork.reveal: the grass runs out, and the line of mothers goes on: the round has no beginning to find.

original.note: Pali anamatagga: without a discoverable beginning. SN 15 is the Anamatagga Samyutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: no beginning to find means the past is long.
what it means: in SN 15.1–2, the round of lives has no discoverable beginning; the grass and the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers.

what a scholar hears: anamatagga is rendered 'whose first point is not known'; the same chapter's line that it is hard to find a being who has not been one's mother is echoed in Tibetan practices for developing compassion.
recall: the way to the far shore

chat.says: Why do some Buddhists say anyone you meet may have been your mother?
options: The round of lives has no findable beginning, so anyone may once have been family.
It's a polite way of reminding people to respect their elders and parents.
Because families are reborn together as a group, life after life.
chat.meaning: SN 15 says the round has no discoverable beginning, so it's hard to find a being who hasn't at some time been your mother or father.

jujube.meaning: a small fruit with a hard seed

Tibet.meaning: a Himalayan land with its own Buddhist teachers

round of wandering.meaning: the long cycle of birth and death

notes: SN 15.1–2 paraphrased. Confirm: grass, sticks, branches and foliage of Jambudipa, cut into pieces four fingers long, laid down 'this is my mother, this my mother's mother'; earth made into balls the size of jujube kernels for fathers.
'The next twenty discourses' assumes SN 15 has about twenty suttas; please check the count.
SN 15.14–19: it is not easy to find a being who has not been one's mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter; confirm the references.
The Tibetan practice of recognizing all beings as mothers (part of the seven-point cause and effect instruction) is described generally; confirm the link drawn to this chapter is fair.
The hook's mail-in DNA test is a modern image, not a claim.
